paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Falcon 9 is a rocket designed and built in the United States by SpaceX. It has two stages, is partly reusable, and is classed as a medium-lift launcher. The first stage, called the booster, lifts the second stage and the payload to a set speed and height; the second stage then carries the payload the rest of the way to its orbit. Both stages use SpaceX Merlin engines, burning very cold liquid oxygen with a rocket-grade kerosene called RP-1.

paragraphs.heading: Flying again
paragraphs.text: A key feature of Falcon 9 is reuse. The booster can come back and land upright so it can fly again, and this was first done on the 20th flight, in December 2015. By November 7, 2026, SpaceX had landed boosters 659 times, and single boosters have flown as many as 37 times. Even the fairing halves drift down under parachutes, are pulled out of the water, and can fly several more times.

paragraphs.heading: Its record
paragraphs.text: Falcon 9 first flew on June 4, 2010. It launched its first Commercial Resupply mission to the International Space Station on October 8, 2012, and in 2020 it became the first commercial rocket to send people to orbit. With 698 successful flights, it has launched more often than any other active rocket, with two failures in flight, one partial failure and one rocket destroyed before flight. In January 2021 a single Falcon 9 carried 143 satellites into orbit, a record for one rocket.

paragraphs.heading: Trusted with big jobs
paragraphs.text: Falcon 9 is rated to carry NASA astronauts to the space station and is certified for the US National Security Space Launch program. NASA's Launch Services Program places it in its low-risk category, which lets it launch the agency's most costly and complex missions. The rocket has gone through several versions, from v1.0 in 2010 to the Block 5 variant flying since May 2018.

paragraphs.heading: How it was paid for
paragraphs.text: SpaceX paid for its previous rocket, Falcon 1, with its own money. Falcon 9 was also built with private money, but NASA had agreed in advance to buy several flights once the rocket showed certain abilities. Under NASA's Commercial Orbital Transportation Services program, a deal first worth US$278 million, later raised to US$396 million, covered three demonstration launches carrying the Dragon cargo spacecraft. In 2008 SpaceX also won a US$1.6 billion contract for at least 12 missions carrying supplies to and from the space station.

paragraphs.heading: Cost and name
paragraphs.text: In 2011 SpaceX put the development cost of the first version at about US$300 million. NASA estimated the same work would have cost US$3.6 billion under a traditional cost-plus contract. The rocket's family name comes from the Millennium Falcon, the starship in the Star Wars films.
